Bill Terms Glossary

Every line item that can appear on a commercial utility bill, explained in plain language with optimization strategies.

  • Kilowatt-hour (kWh)

    A kilowatt-hour is 1000 watts drawn for one hour; it measures energy used, not the rate of use.

    Action: NONE YET

  • Therm

    A therm is 100,000 BTU of heat energy and appears on gas bills; electric bills use kWh instead.

    Action: REDUCE THERMS

  • Billing demand (kW)

    Billing demand is the highest average power draw over a short interval in the period, billed separately from energy.

    Action: SHAVE PEAK

  • Load factor

    Load factor is average demand divided by peak demand for the period; a low ratio means short spikes drive the bill.

    Action: SHAVE PEAK

  • Demand ratchet clause

    A ratchet clause sets billed demand to a floor based on an earlier peak, so a quiet month can still carry a summer charge.

    Action: SHAVE PEAK

  • Power factor penalty

    Some commercial tariffs adjust billing when power factor falls below a stated threshold, because reactive current loads the network.

    Action: CHECK RIDER

  • Fixed customer charge

    A fixed customer charge is billed per period regardless of consumption, so it does not fall when a business closes for a week.

    Action: RIGHTSIZE PLAN

  • Supply vs delivery charges

    Bills commonly separate the cost of energy supplied from the cost of delivering it, and the two can move in opposite directions.

    Action: FIX BILLING_ERROR

  • Rider or surcharge

    A rider is a separate tariff mechanism that adds or credits an amount outside the base rate, often with its own effective dates.

    Action: CHECK RIDER

  • Time-of-use period

    Time-of-use pricing assigns different energy prices to defined hours, so when a business runs equipment changes its cost.

    Action: SHIFT LOAD

  • Peak load contribution tag

    In some markets a customer's draw during a small number of system peak hours sets an obligation that shapes charges for a later year.

    Action: SHAVE PEAK

  • Blended effective rate

    Dividing total charges by billed kWh gives an effective rate that lets two different bills be compared on one number.

    Action: FIX BILLING_ERROR

  • Prorated billing period

    Billing periods are not always the same length, so a 34-day period can look like a usage jump against a 28-day one.

    Action: FIX BILLING_ERROR

  • Estimated meter read

    When a read is unavailable the utility may estimate usage, and a later actual read reconciles the difference into one period.

    Action: FIX BILLING_ERROR

  • Reactive energy (kVARh)

    Reactive energy is the portion of alternating current that oscillates without doing work, and it can appear as its own billed line.

    Action: CHECK RIDER

  • Degree days (HDD / CDD)

    Degree days summarise how far outdoor temperature sat from a base point, and they let two billing periods be compared at equal weather.

    Action: REDUCE THERMS
